findings.body: The light branch changes the prior 30% shade to 70%, producing a very pale link on a light background; the dark branch is correspondingly too dark. The metadata link can lose contrast and become difficult to read.
findings.failure_mode: The generated desktop CSS renders reply metadata links with the opposite intensity from the pre-existing design.
findings.impact: The light branch changes the prior 30% shade to 70%, producing a very pale link on a light background; the dark branch is correspondingly too dark. The metadata link can lose contrast and become difficult to read.
findings.root_cause: The migration inverted the original lightness percentage instead of retaining 30% for the light-theme branch and using its complement only for the dark-theme branch.
findings.title: Preserve the original 30% metadata-link shade
findings.trigger: A desktop user views an embedded or expanded reply whose .topic-meta-data h5 contains a link, under either the standard light scheme or a dark scheme.
findings.verifier_reason: Patch shows line 291 changed from 30% to 70% for light theme. Original was scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%), now dark-light-choose uses 70% for light branch. This inverts the original shade, making links paler on light themes.

findings.body: Names that previously used the stronger 30% primary shade now use exactly the same 50% shade as the title at line 527, removing the intended visual hierarchy and reducing name contrast on both light and dark schemes.
findings.failure_mode: Generated desktop styles render member names with the wrong shade and make them indistinguishable from secondary title text.
findings.impact: Names that previously used the stronger 30% primary shade now use exactly the same 50% shade as the title at line 527, removing the intended visual hierarchy and reducing name contrast on both light and dark schemes.
findings.root_cause: The mechanical dark-theme conversion replaced the existing 30% lightness with 50% in both branches.
findings.title: Desktop group-member names use the title shade instead of the original name shade
findings.trigger: A desktop user opens a group-member listing that renders .group-member-info .name.
findings.verifier_reason: Patch confirms line 522 changed from 30% to 50%/50%. The .name selector previously had 30% lightness, now matches .title at 50%. This removes visual hierarchy between name and title elements.

findings.body: The h3 previously used a strong 20% shade but now uses the same 50%/50% color as the h4 immediately below it. This removes heading hierarchy and can reduce the h3's contrast against the topic-map background.
findings.failure_mode: Generated mobile styles render primary and secondary topic-map headings at the same color intensity.
findings.impact: The h3 previously used a strong 20% shade but now uses the same 50%/50% color as the h4 immediately below it. This removes heading hierarchy and can reduce the h3's contrast against the topic-map background.
findings.root_cause: The conversion replaced the original 20% heading shade with the generic 50% pair.
findings.suggested_fix: Use dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 20%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 80%)), matching the original mobile value and the desktop topic-map h3 rule.
findings.title: Mobile topic-map heading loses its stronger heading shade
findings.trigger: A mobile user views a topic map containing an h3 heading under either a light or dark color scheme.
findings.verifier_reason: Patch confirms line 182 changed from 20% to 50%/50%. Desktop topic-post.scss:321 uses 20%/80% for h3. Mobile h3 now matches h4 at 50%, losing heading hierarchy. Desktop maintains distinction.

raw_findings.failure_mode: The generated mobile dark-theme CSS displays disabled composer content with insufficient foreground/background contrast.
raw_findings.impact: The new dark branch gives the textarea a dark secondary-derived background, while the unchanged text color remains darken($primary, 40%). With a typical light primary and dark secondary, these become similarly dark or mid-tone colors and the disabled draft text is difficult to read.
raw_findings.root_cause: Only the disabled textarea background was switched from a primary-derived light color to a secondary-derived dark color; its explicit foreground color was not adapted to the new background.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Adapt the disabled textarea foreground for dark themes as well, for example by choosing a sufficiently light primary-derived foreground in the dark branch, or retain a background that contrasts with the existing text color.
